children.text: Quezon Bridge is an Art Deco bridge built in 1939 over Manila's Pasig River, linking Quiapo to the north and Ermita to the south. Destroyed in the war and rebuilt close to its original look, it gained new LED lighting in 2022 that makes the evening view much nicer.

Quezon Bridge spans the Pasig River in central Manila, connecting Quezon Boulevard in Quiapo on the north bank with Padre Burgos Avenue in Ermita on the south. Its official name is the Manuel L. Quezon Memorial Bridge, in honor of Manuel Luis Quezon, who was president of the Philippine Commonwealth when it was built. When you walk through old Manila, it is the natural crossing from the Quiapo Church area over the river toward Manila City Hall and Intramuros.

The site was originally occupied by the Puente Colgante (the "hanging bridge"). First called the Puente de Claveria after a governor-general, it was an iron suspension bridge begun in 1849 and opened on January 4, 1852, about
long and
7 m

wide. It crossed the river in a single span with no piers in the water and is described as the first wire-cable suspension bridge built in Asia. It was a toll bridge until the City of Manila bought it in 1911 and the tolls were abolished. But it was too worn to handle growing 20th-century motor traffic, so it was replaced by today's Quezon Bridge in 1939.

Quezon Bridge combines an arch with prestressed concrete girders in an Art Deco style, and is said to have been inspired by the Sydney Harbour Bridge in Australia. Current records give it a length of about
and a width of about

, with two lanes in each direction. When Japanese forces blew up the Pasig River bridges during the 1945 Battle of Manila, this one was destroyed too; unlike Jones Bridge, which was rebuilt as a plain bridge without decoration, Quezon Bridge was rebuilt in 1946 to resemble its prewar design. It has since needed repeated repairs and reinforcement because of age and wear, with a major reconstruction in 1996 and fire damage in 2014. The bridge is reported to have been restricted mainly to light vehicles since then.

Today Quezon Bridge is less a showy attraction than an everyday route for Manila residents and a link in an old-town walk. New LED lighting was switched on in February 2022, making the river view after dusk much more pleasant, and the bridge appears as a setting in the first episode of the Philippine action series 'FPJ's Batang Quiapo', so more people now recognize it. It is hard to linger on the roadway and some surrounding streets are dim, so it works best as a short stop: cross, enjoy the view and take photos, then continue to nearby sights such as Quiapo Church, Escolta and Intramuros. This guide covers the bridge's highlights, a walking order, how to get there, connecting routes nearby and cautions.

blocks.title: Art Deco style and the Sydney Harbour Bridge inspiration

children.text: Quezon Bridge was completed in 1939 in the Art Deco style. It is said to have been inspired by the Sydney Harbour Bridge, and it reflects the tastes of the 1930s Commonwealth era, quite different from the Spanish-period buildings and neoclassical bridges of old Manila. Walk slowly and look at the lines of the railings and structure to get a feel for the style.

A suspension bridge called the Puente Colgante opened here in 1852. Described as Asia's first wire-cable suspension bridge, it is said in some stories to have been designed by Gustave Eiffel, but historians record the Basque-Spanish engineer Matías Menchacatorre as its designer. Looking down at the river and imagining the vanished bridge is part of the fun of this place.

From the bridge you can see the Pasig River and the buildings along both banks, upstream and downstream. Ayala Bridge lies close upstream and MacArthur Bridge downstream, so it is also a good place to compare Manila's river bridges. For safety, take photos from the sidewalk and never step into the middle of the roadway.

On the evening of February 12, 2022, the City of Manila held a lighting ceremony for the new LED lights. The mayor and vice mayor led the event, and reports say traffic was opened across the bridge once the lights came on. Around sunset is a good time to see the bridge's outline after dark, but surrounding streets can be dim, so go with company.

blocks.title: The link between Quiapo and Ermita

children.text: The north end of the bridge is Quezon Boulevard in Quiapo and the south end is Padre Burgos Avenue in Ermita. The north side leads to Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda, the south side toward Manila City Hall and Intramuros, so you can feel the contrast between the two districts on foot. The shift from Quiapo's busy street stalls to the south side with government buildings and parks is compressed into one crossing.

blocks.title: The Black Nazarene feast and Quezon Bridge

children.text: The route of the Black Nazarene procession (Traslacion) on January 9 each year around Quiapo includes this bridge. In January 2026 reports, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) National Capital Region office rated four bridges on the route, including this one, in fair condition and said it had no objection to them being used for the procession, on the condition that no vehicles pass along the whole stretch during it. Rehabilitation work on this bridge was reported to be under way at the time. During the feast the bridge is crowded with devotees and closed to traffic, so check the schedule.

The bridge appears as a setting in the first episode of the popular Philippine action series 'FPJ's Batang Quiapo' and again in later episodes. If you have watched the show, seeing the bridge together with the Quiapo area can be a fun extra.
Start at the north end of the bridge on Quezon Boulevard in Quiapo. Seeing Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda first and then walking over makes a natural flow.
Walk slowly across the bridge along the sidewalk. Look at the lines of the railings and structure and glance alternately upstream and downstream. The bridge is known to be about
long, so the crossing takes a little while.
Arrive at Padre Burgos Avenue at the south end. Look around Manila City Hall and the riverside walkway and capture the light around sunset.
After dark, take another look at the bridge with its LED lights on, then head back to your hotel by taxi or Grab before it gets too dark.
The bridge is busy with vehicles, so travel times vary a lot with traffic. Sunset time changes with the season, so check the time for the day.
Start at Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda and take in the atmosphere of devotion to the Black Nazarene.
Cross Quezon Bridge toward Ermita.
Look around the Manila Metropolitan Theater and the old-town buildings.
Head to Intramuros, have lunch and walk the walled city.
Return to your hotel by taxi or Grab. Adjust the schedule to local conditions.
Take a taxi or Grab from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to old Manila. Travel time and fare vary greatly with traffic, so confirm locally.
From a hotel in Manila, set 'Quiapo' or 'Quezon Bridge' as your destination in a taxi or Grab.
Old Manila gets very congested during rush hour.
Carriedo Station on LRT-1 is said to be the closest on the Quiapo side, while UN Avenue Station on the Ermita side may be a fair walk from the bridge.
Check the exact distance and route from the station to the bridge on a map app, then walk.
Quiapo Church, Escolta and Intramuros are within walking distance of one another. In the heat and at night, a taxi or Grab is safer even for short distances.

Quezon Bridge is an outdoor place you see on foot, so the dry season, with little rain and cooler weather, is best for walking. Around sunset the light is soft and you can also see the lights come on.
During the Black Nazarene feast on January 9 each year, the Quiapo area and the surroundings of this bridge get very crowded and can be closed off. If you want to avoid that, adjust your dates.

There are no hotels or restaurants on Quezon Bridge itself. The usual approach is to stay around Quiapo, Ermita, Malate or Intramuros and visit the bridge on foot. For safety and easy transport, choose lodging close to a main road.

Around Quiapo, near the bridge, there are many old street stalls and local eateries. Check hygiene before eating street food, and it is safer to buy bottled water. Opening hours and prices change, so confirm locally.
Visiting around sunset gives good light and a chance to see the lights, but do not stay long after dark.
The bridge has heavy vehicle traffic, so always stay on the sidewalk and do not stand on the roadway.
Hang your phone and camera around your neck or hold them firmly, and keep your wallet in a front pocket to guard against pickpockets.
Combining it with Quiapo Church, Escolta and Intramuros makes an efficient half-day route.
Expect road closures and huge crowds during the January 9 Black Nazarene procession, so check the latest announcements.
In the hot months of March–May, bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
The bridge's condition and traffic restrictions can change, so check on-site signs and the latest news.
Quezon Bridge has had a light-vehicle restriction since the 2014 fire damage and repair work continues, so check on-site signs and the latest announcements.
It is a busy road, so stay off the roadway and cross only at signals and crossings.
Some surrounding streets are dark after sunset, so avoid staying long alone.
Beware of pickpockets and snatchers, and do not show valuables.

Traffic restrictions and repair schedules for the bridge can change. On October 19, 2025, vehicle traffic was temporarily closed from 4:00 a.m. for the Pasig River Esplanade inauguration, so check the latest news around events.
Crowds during the Black Nazarene feast can lead to accidents, so be careful.
The church of the Black Nazarene just north of the bridge, and the center of devotion to the Black Nazarene.

A former commercial street north of the Pasig River whose old buildings remain, a good addition to an old-town walk.
